subject: Does a rolling migration day count as covered? — SOC 2 timeframe question
messages:
From: Samir Patel <samir.patel@nimbushealth.com>
To: Tessa Morgan <tessa.morgan@redwood.com>, Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.com>
Date: Thu, 11 Jun 2026 09:12:00 -0700
Subject: SOC 2 question: our May 15 migration — is that day counted in the report window?

Hi Tessa / Marissa,

Quick question as we're finishing the procurement packet for Nimbus Health: our production migration to a new data partitioning scheme happened on 2026-05-15. The migration was scheduled at 00:30 — 02:00 local time and included a short maintenance window; some system events (db writes replays) landed at 01:45.

For your SOC 2 Type II that lists the period 2026-01-01 through 2026-05-31, should we treat anything that occurred on 2026-05-15 as within the covered period by default, or do you need point-in-time evidence showing state at a specific timestamp? The buyer (Nimbus) is asking whether a mid-month migration day counts as fully covered or whether there are extra evidentiary steps.

We can produce the migration timeline and a minimal log extract but want to avoid an unnecessary evidence dump if you already treat month-end inclusivity broadly.

Thanks — Samir
Samir Patel
Head of Partnerships, Nimbus Health
(samir.patel@nimbushealth.com)

From: Tessa Morgan <tessa.morgan@redwood.com>

Subject: Re: SOC 2 question: our May 15 migration — is that day counted in the report window?

Hi Samir,

Thanks for the note and the timeline. Short answer up-front: the SOC 2 Type II period (2026-01-01 through 2026-05-31) is inclusive of May 31st, and anything that occurred on 2026-05-15 falls within the reported period. That said, auditors sometimes request point-in-time evidence for events that affect control state mid-period (migrations, large schema changes, etc.).

To avoid back-and-forth: we typically provide a bridge letter that documents the nature of the migration and confirms that the change did not modify control intent or operating effectiveness (or, if it did, we surface compensating controls). We also provide a concise set of logs / snapshots around the migration window (for example: system-state at 2026-05-15T00:00:00Z and a rolling log extract 00:30–02:30 local) so auditors can inspect exact timestamps.

I've looped in Karthik on the logs and Marissa on the bridge letter draft. Lydia from Brightline (our auditor) — if you can confirm whether the timeline+bridge approach is sufficient or whether you need additional point-in-time artifacts, that'd be great.

Attached: draft Bridge_Letter_Draft.docx (internal draft), proposed evidence index (evidence_index.csv).

Best,
Tessa Morgan

Hi Tessa / Samir,

Thanks for the clear context. Confirming from the audit perspective: when a SOC 2 Type II report lists a period through 2026-05-31, the period is inclusive — activities that occurred on 2026-05-15 are within scope. However, auditors assess whether a change materially affects control operation during the period. For a migration that included a maintenance window, we typically ask for two things:

- A brief bridge letter describing the migration purpose, the systems impacted, and an assertion about whether control objectives were preserved (e.g., "no changes to access control processes; no new privileged accounts created").
- Time-bounded evidence: a small set of system-state snapshots or logs around the migration window (we usually request timezone-normalized timestamps in UTC). For example: system snapshot at 2026-05-15T00:00:00Z and rolling logs 2026-05-15T00:30:00Z–2026-05-15T02:30:00Z.

If you can provide signed bridge-letter language + the indexed logs (CSV or log extracts) and an explanation of whether any fallbacks/replays occurred, that will usually be sufficient. If the migration introduced a new control or a permanent configuration change that affects scope (rare), we would ask for additional documentation.

I'm attaching our short guidance PDF (audit_evidence_requirements.pdf) that lists preferred formats and redaction guidance. Also: please ensure timestamps are explicit about timezone — auditors will convert everything to UTC for review, and ambiguous local timestamps cause extra questions.

Happy to accept the materials to the Google Drive folder Tessa linked and confirm once we've completed the review.

Regards,
Lydia Chen
Senior Auditor, Brightline Assurance
(audits@brightline.com)
